title: Sigma Notation
short: Σ is shorthand for adding the terms of a pattern.
trouble: Students miscount the terms when the index does not start at 1.

blocks.html: Adding up the terms of a sequence from Recursive Formulas is so common that it has its own symbol, the Greek capital letter sigma, $\Sigma$, for "sum."
$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} f(k) = f(m) + f(m + 1) + \cdots + f(n)$$ Plug in each whole number $k$ from $m$ to $n$ and add the results. The number of terms is $n - m + 1$.

Sigma notation is a compact recipe: the expression after $\Sigma$ makes each term, and the numbers below and above say where the index starts and stops. Counting the terms: from $m$ to $n$ there are $n - m$ steps, but both ends count, so there are $n - m + 1$ terms, just as there are 3 numbers from 5 to 7.

blocks.title: Counting terms
blocks.q: How many terms are in $\displaystyle\sum_{k=4}^{20} k^2$?

blocks.title: Writing a sum in sigma notation
steps: The terms go up by 4, so the general term is $4k + c$. With $k = 1$ the term is 3, so $c = -1$.
There are 5 terms, so $k$ runs from 1 to 5. Check: $4(5) - 1 = 19$.

blocks.html: Two handy facts: a constant added $N$ times is $N$ times the constant, so $\sum_{k=1}^{10} 4 = 40$; and sums split, so $\sum (a_k + b_k) = \sum a_k + \sum b_k$ and $\sum c\,a_k = c\sum a_k$. They follow from regrouping and factoring an ordinary sum.

Miscounting terms when the index doesn't start at 1. $\sum_{k=4}^{20}$ has 17 terms, not 16 and not 20. Another slip is starting the substitution at $k = 1$ out of habit. Always begin with the number written under the sigma.
